Hi, I got Claude to port autoCorres2 to LEAN: https://github.com/eisbaw/Clift

autoCorres was used to lift the C code in seL4 to Isabelle - over 200k lines of proofs back before AI.
Impressive stuff. Yet I want to adopt this methodology in modern setting and using AI to do the heavy proof work.

There are a bunch of C examples in the repo, 3 of which are not yet proven.

I guess I am writing this to:

  1. Say hello.
  2. I did a thing -- Clift. Made by Claude over some 5 days of ~continious operation.
  3. Hints for the remaining difficult proofs.

I tried to find the first key proof "gcd_correct_nat: C gcd() computes GCD over natural numbers (full pipeline, zero sorry)" in the repo, but failed to do so. Can you say, where I can find the statement?

The closest thing I found is here where it says "The proof is mechanically straightforward but extremely verbose (~200+ lines) due to the complex L1 result set structure.". But I cannot find the actual proof. Can you point me to where the proof is?
(Also note that the l2_gcd_spec theorem in this file is trivial since l2_gcd is defined basically as the conclusion of the statement).
but you may right that it is insufficient.

You're absolutely right -- as Claude would put it :-)
This at least looks the part: https://github.com/eisbaw/Clift/commit/ba4fad0b0f5dd8bc922bfa90469ac5987455c915
With all this AI, there will be some false claims -- that is why I want to use Lean.
Is there deterministic tooling available to check for tautological or self-referential proofs?

(Draft paper here: https://github.com/eisbaw/Clift/blob/master/paper/clift.pdf.)

If this all checks out, this would be a great addition to the Lean ecosystem! See also #Program verification > AutoCorres in Lean where I made a far less ambitious PoC to test whether mvcgen could be used for VC generation. It can, so I would suggest you use Std.Do.Triple to express validHoare instead and use mvcgen to prove lemmas such as auto_l1_gcd_body_validHoare. That would get rid of stuff like simp only [L1.seq] and it might also help with the kernel reduction issue.

Any reason why you kept targeting CSimpl from CImporter? I just had a call today with industry users and got some feedback on their use of AutoCorres2 to verify crypto applications and they considered the existence of CSimpl a legacy artifact. You could define a denotational semantics on some representation of the C AST that maps into the SpecM monad (that you don't seem to define explicitly, only NondetM)? I guess that amounts to moving the L1 translation into CImporter and absorbing L1corres proofs into the trusted code base. That doesn't seem too bad to me compared to the reduction in complexity.

From the vibe-README

The proofs apply to the actual C code, not a rewrite or model

...Isn't the point of this project to provide a formal model that C programs can be automatically rewritten into? Especially given that the CImporter README explicitly states that it is in the TCB? Lol?

@Markus de Medeiros well, if you look at the lean-zip project for example, there is a reimplementation of the C code in lean - a copy so there is a real risk of drift. The aim here is get rid of the drift, by automatically lifting the actual C code into lean so we can better reason. I dont think it claims to have a proven CImporter, so it is trusted - just like clang is. Not so lol to me IMHO

@Sebastian Graf thanks for your feedback! I find Claude struggling to refactor proofs into smaller pieces that don't hit the lean kernel stack depth limits. Wide C structs with many fields really expose some scaling issues - with this approach - in the lean kernel. Do you expect these to be ameliorated by using mvcgen approach?

Huh, that wide C structs cause scaling issues in the kernel rather than the elaborator is news to me. Can you maybe instruct Claude to provide an MWE? If it's indeed just scaling issues in the tactic elaborator for some tactics, then mvcgen and the upcoming SymM-based tactic framework might help.

Mark Ruvald Pedersen said:

The aim here is get rid of the drift, by automatically lifting the actual C code into lean

Yeah but this does involve specifying a model of C programs and you can ask obvious questions about it (Like, what variant of the C? C99? ISO? CompCert? Do the model semantics match the behavior of clang or gcc, or whatever compiler I'm using to run the "actual" code? Does the model include system calls? When I type size_t how many bits do I expect it to have in its Lean model?). Anyways, do whatever you want but this just strikes me as bizarre.
